summary: Benchmark bar research in progress. Verified authority pages for 3 of 8 topics via direct fetches (EIA 'Electricity use in homes', EIA 'Prices and factors affecting prices', Con Edison 'How to Read Your Bill'). web_search tool is broken this run (returns identical irrelevant results for every query — not usable); web_fetch budget exhausted at 15. findings: FACT — EIA 'Electricity use in homes' (https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/use-of-energy/electricity-use-in-homes.php, retrieved 2026-08-27): narrative structure with embedded click-to-enlarge charts, 'did you know?' data callouts, and explicit data provenance. Cites 2020 RECS: avg US household 10,500 kWh/yr; end-use shares AC 19%, space heating 12%, water heating 12%; 89% homes use AC vs 57% in 1980; 67% central AC vs 27% in 1980; 34% homes have 2+ refrigerators; avg refrigerator operating cost $87/yr (2020). Depth approx 1,500+ words. Data format: survey-statistics + share-of-end-use breakdown, not dollar figures.

FACT — EIA 'Prices and factors affecting prices' (https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/prices-and-factors-affecting-prices.php, retrieved 2026-08-27): structure = factor list (fuels, power-plant costs, transmission/distribution, weather, regulations) + 'did you know?' callout ('cost of generating electricity is the largest component of the price') + charts. Depth moderate. Key data point: prices generally highest in summer (truncated before full stat).

FACT — Con Edison 'How to Read Your Bill' (https://www.coned.com/en/accounts-billing/your-bill/how-to-read-your-bill, retrieved 2026-08-27): utility help-center structure = 3 charge categories (supply / delivery / taxes) each with 'What it is / How it works / Important to know' subsections; sample bills for 3 customer classes (residential, small-medium business, large business); FAQ accordions (delayed billing, NY State Energy Bill Credit); downloadable PDFs (customer rights, average monthly bills). Delivers the utility's own 2026 figure: >$3.2B in local energy-infrastructure taxes expected 2026, ~quarter of delivery charge is local taxes.

INFERENCE — The authority-page bar is data-provenance-driven: EIA pages cite named surveys (RECS) with year and exact statistics; utility pages cite their own tariff/rate/fee structure. Pages without named, dated data sources are below the bar. The site's own thin pages (e.g. 41-how-to-read-electricity-bill.md, 404 words, 3 sources, 0 tables) already cite Con Edison but lack sample-bill visuals, FAQ accordions, and PDF downloads that the authority page carries.

INFERENCE — shared formatting standards visible so far: (1) named/dated data citations; (2) data-callout boxes ('did you know?'); (3) visual formats (charts, sample-bill images, PDFs); (4) FAQ accordions; (5) related-content navigation to deeper resources. Full 5-standard list requires the remaining 5 topics.

OBSERVATION — energy.gov/energysaver/* subtree is 404ing as of retrieval date (all cited URLs from the site's own articles, e.g. /energysaver/heat-and-cool, /energysaver/save-electricity-and-fuel/lighting-choices-save-you-money/led-lighting, /energysaver/energy-saver-guide-2022, all HTTP 404). energy.gov root redirects /energysaver to homepage. The site's 03-why-is-my-electric-bill-so-high.md cites 6 energy.gov URLs that are now dead — a concrete freshness/authority risk for the audit.
